Create a scalar UDF with {{c1::CREATE FUNCTION}} dbo.CalculateSalesTax(@Amount DECIMAL(10,2), @TaxRate DECIMAL(5,4)) RETURNS DECIMAL(10,2) AS BEGIN RETURN @Amount * @TaxRate; END;
column2:
The function accepts two values and returns their product using its declared result type.
Review source

column1: Declare a tax function's result type with {{c1::RETURNS DECIMAL(10,2)}} in its header.
column2:
The return type specifies a decimal result with two fractional digits.
Review source

column1: Return a scalar variable's value with {{c1::RETURN @TaxAmount}}; inside the function body.
column2:
This is the function's calculated result, not a stored-procedure status code.
Review source

column1: Call dbo.CalculateSalesTax for Amount and TaxRate columns with SELECT {{c1::dbo.CalculateSalesTax(Amount, TaxRate)}} FROM dbo.Orders;
column2:
Fabric Warehouse scalar UDFs are in preview and must qualify for inlining in SELECT...FROM queries on user tables.
Review source | Fabric Warehouse

column1: A parameterless scalar UDF call still needs {{c1::parentheses}}, as in SELECT dbo.GetCode();
column2:
The parentheses are required even when the argument list is empty.
Review source

column1: The tenure calculation's call to {{c1::GETDATE()}} introduces nondeterminism.
column2:
The system clock can change even when the function's explicit arguments remain the same.
Review source

column1: To make a date calculation repeatable, pass its {{c1::as-of date}} as an argument instead of reading GETDATE().
column2:
Use deterministic operations for the remaining calculation.
Review source

column1: SQL Server requires {{c1::SCHEMABINDING}} for a T-SQL UDF to be marked deterministic.
column2:
Schema binding alone is not enough if the function uses nondeterministic operations.
Review source

column1: SELECT DATEDIFF(YEAR, '20241231', '20250101'); returns {{c1::1}}.
column2:
One year boundary passes, although only one day elapses.
Review source

column1: In SQL Server 2019 and later, automatic scalar UDF inlining requires database compatibility level {{c1::150 or higher}}.
column2:
Inlining must also be enabled, and the function and calling query must qualify.
Review source

column1: A T-SQL scalar UDF can assign local variables but cannot directly update {{c1::permanent database tables}}.
column2:
The function body must not change permanent database state.
Review source

column1: Modify the existing definition with {{c1::ALTER FUNCTION}} dbo.CalculateSalesTax(@Amount DECIMAL(10,2), @TaxRate DECIMAL(5,4)) RETURNS DECIMAL(10,2) AS BEGIN RETURN @Amount * @TaxRate; END;
column2:
ALTER FUNCTION preserves permissions instead of dropping and recreating the object.
Review source

column1: Skip removal of a missing function with DROP FUNCTION {{c1::IF EXISTS}} dbo.CalculateSalesTax;
column2:
Available in SQL Server 2016 and later, this does not suppress other reasons that a drop can fail.
Review source

column1: Inspect recorded object references in {{c1::sys.sql_expression_dependencies}} before removing a scalar UDF.
column2:
Dependency review helps identify callers that require attention.
Review source

column1: The formatted phone value '(123) 456-7890' needs {{c1::14}} ASCII characters of return capacity.
column2:
The ten digits gain two parentheses, one space, and one hyphen.
Review source

column1: To use a scalar UDF parameter's default in a SELECT expression, pass {{c1::DEFAULT}} in that argument position.
column2:
Unlike a stored-procedure argument, a UDF argument is not simply omitted in an expression call.
